<meta>This page continues the first letter from Spartacus (Adam Weishaupt) to Cato (Xavier von Zwack), beginning on page 1. The "5)" catchword suggests continuity with the fifth point or a following section.</meta>

1) I would look around for established, active, and industrious men. I believe (24.) 3 = = <note>These symbols and numbers likely refer to a specific member or a grade within the Order's hierarchy.</note> should not be neglected. You will read the rest of my project in my letter to Celsus <note>A pseudonym for a member of the Order, often identified as the physician Johann Jakob Herzog.</note>.

2) In the meetings, I would place people at the head who possess prestige and authority, and who understand how to set the tone for the way of thinking; men who are revered as an oracle <note>original: *Oracul*</note> by the youth, and who are additionally serious and strict in their morals.

3) I would have the recruitment <note>original: *Rekrutirung*</note> carried out by specific, capable people who also understand how to manage the training <note>original: *Abrichtung*; implies a disciplined, almost military-style drilling</note> of the members. Pliny <note>original: *Plinius*; pseudonym for an unidentified member</note> and Pythagoras <note>Pseudonym for a member, possibly Franz Georg von Werdenstein</note> possess excellent skill in this regard.

4) Those who are far too lukewarm and negligent, people of bad morals and reputation—or even those with heads far too "moist" <note>original: *feuchte Köpfe*; an 18th-century German idiom likely referring to drunkards or people with "soft" or unreliable intellects</note>—I would seek to remove, not through direct exclusion <note>original: *Excluſion*</note>, but rather I would bring them to the point of requesting their own dismissal by overwhelming them with work and obligations. Alternatively, I would unite them all into a dedicated meeting under equally negligent superiors <note>original: *Superioren*</note>; then it will surely fall apart on its own. Those who are slightly less unsuitable I would leave entirely unattended and cease writing to them.

5) A clever tactic <note>original: *Hauptkunſtgriff*; literally a "master stroke" or "chief artifice"</note> is that the newly admitted member must not be allowed to enjoy all the advantages, acquaintances, and company of the veterans <note>The "veterans" refers to long-standing members of the Order who have attained higher degrees of initiation.</note> immediately upon their first entry.

6) I would distribute the young people among established, educated men for their instruction <note>original: *Unterricht*; this refers to the systematic mentoring and ideological training required of new initiates.</note>.

7) Those to whom they are assigned for instruction should never make themselves familiar with their subordinates; they should let themselves be sought out. <note>This instruction emphasizes maintaining a sense of mystery and hierarchy; by remaining distant, the superiors appear more authoritative and desirable to emulate.</note>

8) Primarily, however, it depends on which people they admit into the <term>Illuminati</term> Class <note>The *Illuminaten-Grad* or Class was a specific rank within Weishaupt’s hierarchy, situated between the preparatory "Minerval" degrees and the higher "Mystery" degrees.</note>: if these are well-chosen, then things can go quite well. But I believe they must provide new blood to the sickly body. If new, previously unknown, distinguished, and respectable persons appear in this class, they will experience the most pleasant consequences from it.

9) Above all, the goodness of the cause is recommended by one's own example; one must be—or at least appear to be—exactly what one wishes to make of others. Nothing harms the good cause more than when words do not match deeds: they must honor and respect one another, speak well of one another, meet people with kindness and affection, and express to them that they are concerned for their best interests. Imperceptibly, those around them will adopt their customs <note>original: *Sitten*; refers to the moral conduct and social habits encouraged by the Order.</note> and gain affection—

<summary>Weishaupt outlines the importance of hierarchy, social distance between ranks, and the necessity of recruiting "respectable" individuals to revitalize the Order. In general, you must break your people of the habit of blabbing and revealing the identities of the members; through this, almost our greatest strength is lost. National [Superior], under the name National Lodge <note>original: National ☐; the square symbol denotes a lodge or administrative assembly.</note>. This reports to the
->General.<-

After the Directing Illuminatus <note>original: Post illum. dirigentem</note>, one becomes a **Priest**. Those beneath him who work purely in scholarly pursuits <note>original: in Scientificis; within the Order, this referred to the gathering of information and the educational training of members</note> remain simple Priests. Those capable of administration then become **Provincial Consultants** <note>original: Consultores Provincialis</note>, **Provincial**, and consequently **Regent**. Whatever the Provincial receives regarding scholarly matters, he passes to his corresponding class; whatever else occurs in administration, he decides upon.

# XI.

## An Original Declaration of Obligation. <note>The German term 'Revers' refers to a formal, legally binding written promise or declaration of duty.</note>

I, the undersigned, pledge upon my honor and good name—renouncing all mental reservations <note>A standard legal and ecclesiastical phrase meaning the signer is not secretly intending to break the oath while making it.</note>—concerning those matters entrusted to me by Baron Frauenberg regarding my admission into a secret society, that I shall never reveal the slightest detail to anyone, even to my closest friend or relative, in any possible way, whether through words, signs, looks, etc. <note>The original uses '2c.', an archaic abbreviation for 'etc.'</note>, regardless of whether my admission is ultimately finalized or not; all the more so as my initiator <note>In the German 'Aufnehmer,' meaning the person receiving him into the order.</note> has assured me that nothing against the State, Religion, or good morals shall be undertaken within this society. I also promise to immediately return any writings shared with me or letters received for this purpose, after having made the necessary extracts—which shall be intelligible to no one else.

And all of this, as truly as I am an honest man, and intend to remain so.

->Ingolstadt, August 5,<-
->1784.<-
